stem: Which statement about how the body regulates calcium is true?
choices: Calcitonin comes from the thyroid when calcium rises and reverses PTH's effects on bone
Calcitonin comes from the parathyroids when calcium rises and reverses PTH's effects on bone
PTH raises blood calcium by making the kidney excrete more calcium
Vitamin D, the long-term regulator of calcium, is activated in the liver
ex: PTH is the fast-acting regulator: osteoclast resorption, calcium reabsorption in the kidney and calcitriol so the gut absorbs calcium. Vitamin D, activated in the kidney, is the long-term one. Calcitonin, from the thyroid when calcium rises, reverses PTH's effects on bone cells.
why: Calcitonin is the thyroid's answer to high calcium: it reverses PTH's effects on bone cells.
Calcitonin is made in the thyroid (its C cells); the parathyroids make PTH.
PTH makes the kidney reabsorb calcium, not excrete it.
Dr. Taylor's slide has vitamin D activated in the kidney.

stem: Which statement about thyroid disease and dental care is true?
choices: Hypothyroidism in children delays eruption; hyperthyroidism accelerates it
Hyperthyroidism in children delays eruption; hypothyroidism accelerates it
Hypothyroidism brings tachycardia and heat intolerance, so limit vasoconstrictor
Hyperthyroidism brings macroglossia and delayed wound healing
ex: Hyperthyroid: weight loss, tachycardia, heat intolerance, more sensitivity to epinephrine (avoid excessive vasoconstrictor when uncontrolled), accelerated eruption. Hypothyroid, seen far more often: fatigue, weight gain, bradycardia, delayed eruption, macroglossia, delayed wound healing.
why: Too little thyroid hormone slows eruption; too much speeds it up.
That swaps them: hyperthyroidism accelerates eruption and hypothyroidism delays it.
Tachycardia, heat intolerance and epinephrine sensitivity belong to uncontrolled hyperthyroidism.
Macroglossia and delayed wound healing are findings of hypothyroidism.

stem: Which statement about a patient with Addison disease in the dental chair is false?
choices: The oral pigmentation comes from low ACTH stimulating melanocytes
Hypotension, fatigue and hyperpigmentation are typical
A long or stressful surgery can trigger an adrenal crisis, so the steroid dose may be raised
Severe hypotension and confusion are signs of an adrenal crisis
ex: Addison disease: hypotension, fatigue and hyperpigmentation, with diffuse oral melanosis because high ACTH stimulates melanocytes. Long or stressful surgery, infection, trauma or a missed steroid dose can trigger an adrenal crisis.
why: This is the false one: ACTH is high in Addison disease, and the high ACTH stimulates the melanocytes.
This is true: those are the findings on Dr. Taylor's slide.
This is true: after a big procedure the patient may need extra corticosteroid, the dose set with the physician.
This is true: severe hypotension, weakness, confusion, loss of consciousness and shock.

stem: Which statement about diabetes and the mouth is false?
choices: Periodontal disease affects glycemic control, but not the other way around
Xerostomia, candidiasis and burning mouth syndrome are oral findings
Decreased neutrophil function and a poor blood supply are reasons diabetic wounds heal poorly
An HbA1c above 7 percent raises the risk of implant failure
ex: Diabetes in the mouth: xerostomia, candidiasis, burning mouth syndrome, delayed healing, more periodontal disease and caries. The periodontal link runs both ways. Poor healing comes from decreased neutrophil function, poor blood supply and impaired collagen synthesis.
why: This is the false one: the link is bidirectional; diabetes worsens periodontal disease, and periodontal inflammation worsens glycemic control.
This is true: all three are on Dr. Taylor's list of oral manifestations.

stem: Diabetes insipidus is the disorder Dr. Taylor lists under which hormone?

Insulin, the beta-cell hormone that moves glucose into cells
Oxytocin, the other posterior pituitary hormone
Aldosterone, the adrenal cortex hormone that retains sodium

why: ADH conserves water, and diabetes insipidus is listed under it.

stem: Growth hormone is still made after puberty. According to Dr. Taylor, what stops it from lengthening the long bones?
choices: The sex hormones of puberty fuse the growth plates
The pituitary stops making growth hormone at puberty
Rising thyroid hormone at puberty closes the bone ends
Cortisol from the adrenal cortex blocks growth hormone's receptors
ex: Growth hormone is strongest in childhood and adolescence but persists for life. The sex hormones of puberty fuse the growth plates, so afterward growth hormone no longer lengthens the long bones. That is why GH excess before puberty makes a very tall person, and after puberty it causes acromegaly.
why: His answer to the class: puberty's sex hormones fuse the growth plates, so growth hormone no longer lengthens the long bones.
He said the opposite: growth hormone stays at some level throughout life, strongest in childhood and adolescence.
Thyroid hormone runs metabolism in his lecture; he credited the sex hormones with fusing the plates.
Cortisol handles stress, immunity and glucose in his lecture; it isn't what ends long-bone growth.

likely.t: Acromegaly's growing jaw (Class I to Class III, diastemas, macroglossia); growth plates fused by the sex hormones, and implant timing

stem: A 12-year-old boy lost a maxillary incisor in an accident at 10, and his family asks when an implant can go in. What does Dr. Taylor's reasoning say?
choices: Wait until his growth has stopped, because an implant stays fixed while the face grows around it
Place it now, because an implant in a child moves down with the growing jaw like a natural tooth
Place it once all his permanent teeth have erupted, since eruption marks the end of facial growth
Wait until growth hormone has disappeared from his blood, around age 25
ex: The sex hormones of puberty fuse the growth plates and end the growth period. Dr. Taylor estimates when that will be (a 13- or 14-year-old boy with hair on his upper lip is near puberty and near his final height) and plans the implant for after it, because an implant fixed in growing bone ends up out of place as the face grows around it.
why: He won't place an implant while the face and body are still growing: the implant is stuck in the bone while everything moves around it.
An implant is fixed in the bone; it doesn't erupt or move with growth, which is exactly the problem.
Eruption isn't his marker; he looks at puberty and the end of the growth period.
Growth hormone persists for life; what ends growth is the sex hormones fusing the growth plates.

likely.t: Acromegaly's growing jaw (Class I to Class III, diastemas, macroglossia); growth plates fused by the sex hormones, and implant timing

stem: How should the dentist approach her local anesthetic, and why?
choices: Use epinephrine cautiously: she may be overly sensitive to it, and it raises heart rate and blood pressure
Add extra epinephrine: her thyroid disease slows the heart, so a stronger vasoconstrictor will keep her pulse up
Confirm she has eaten and taken her medication first, and keep a fast-acting carbohydrate ready in case her glucose drops
Avoid epinephrine completely, because a vasoconstrictor in thyroid disease can set off an adrenal crisis in the chair
ex: Hyperthyroid patients may be excessively sensitive to sympathomimetic drugs, and excess epinephrine raises heart rate and blood pressure; hers are already 116 and 146 over 90. So use epinephrine-containing anesthetics cautiously and avoid excessive vasoconstrictor while her disease is uncontrolled.

stem: In a thyroidectomy or parathyroidectomy, which nerve does the surgeon identify first, and what does damage to it cause?
choices: The recurrent laryngeal nerve; a hoarse, raspy voice that is usually permanent
The hypoglossal nerve; a tongue that deviates and can't be moved normally
The facial nerve; drooping of one whole side of the face, including the lips
The phrenic nerve; paralysis of half of the diaphragm and shortness of breath
ex: The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs through the thyroid area, so surgeons find it first in thyroid and parathyroid operations. Injury paralyzes half of the vocal cords, leaving a hoarse, raspy voice that is usually permanent. Like the vagus, it runs to several places; he has seen it damaged in heart surgery too.
why: Damage paralyzes half of the vocal cords, so the patient can't make word sounds normally; it is typically permanent.

The facial nerve runs through the parotid, not the thyroid, and its injury changes facial expression, not the voice.
The phrenic nerve drives the diaphragm; he named the nerve whose injury paralyzes half the vocal cords.

likely.t: Hyperthyroid versus hypothyroid dental considerations (hypothyroidism far more common), and the recurrent laryngeal nerve in thyroid surgery

stem: A patient with poorly controlled Graves disease develops a fever, a pulse of 150, agitation and nausea in the chair. What did Dr. Taylor say to do?

Give a fast-acting carbohydrate, then recheck the pulse

Plan extra corticosteroid with her physician after the visit

Capacitation, which ends after the first sperm binds

ex: Binding ZP2 sets off the cortical (zonal) reaction: the oocyte releases its cortical granules and the remaining zona proteins are shed, so no other sperm can bind. That prevents polyspermy: one sperm fertilizes one egg.
why: Cortical granules are released and the remaining zona proteins shed, so no other sperm can bind.
The acrosomal reaction lets a sperm through the zona pellucida; it doesn't block the others.
Capacitation readies sperm in the female tract; it doesn't block a second sperm.
hCG appears days later, from the trophoblasts of the blastocyst, and rescues the corpus luteum.

likely.t: Fertilization: ZP3 sets off the acrosomal reaction, the sperm then binds ZP2, the oocyte finishes its second meiotic division, and the cortical reaction blocks polyspermy

stem: Ejaculated sperm can't fertilize an ovum right away. What has to happen first, and why?
choices: Capacitation: the female tract removes cholesterol from the sperm membrane, so the acrosome can react
Spermatogenesis: the sperm complete their meiotic divisions in the uterus, so they become haploid
The cortical reaction: the sperm shed their tails in the fallopian tube, so they can enter the oocyte
Decidualization: the sperm gain adhesion molecules in the uterus, so they can bind the endometrium
ex: In the male tract, cholesterol-rich vesicles keep the sperm membrane rigid, so the acrosome can't rupture too early. In the female tract the sperm lose those inhibitory factors: cholesterol leaves the membrane, calcium can enter, and the acrosomal reaction becomes possible. That is capacitation.
why: Capacitation removes the cholesterol lock and the blocking proteins, so the acrosomal reaction can happen after ZP3 binding.
Sperm are already haploid when ejaculated; it is the oocyte that finishes its second meiotic division at fertilization.
The cortical reaction is the oocyte's, and it blocks extra sperm; sperm don't shed their tails to get ready.
Decidualization is a change in the endometrium for implantation, not in the sperm.

stem:
Which statements about capacitation are true?
1. Cholesterol and other sterols are removed from the sperm membrane, making it more fluid.
2. The membrane potential changes so calcium can enter the sperm.
3. The tail's beat changes from whip-like to wave-like.
4. Proteins and carbohydrates that would block the egg-binding sites are removed.
ex: His slide lists four changes: sterols such as cholesterol (and glycoproteins) leave the membrane, blocking proteins and carbohydrates are removed, the membrane potential changes so calcium can enter for the acrosomal reaction, and hyperactivation begins, a change from a wave-like to a whip-like beat.
why: It leaves out 4, which is true: proteins and carbohydrates that would block the egg-binding sites are removed.
It includes 3, which is false: hyperactivation goes the other way, from a wave-like to a whip-like beat.
Statements 1, 2 and 4 are true. Statement 3 is false: hyperactivation changes the beat from wave-like to whip-like, not the reverse.
It includes 3, which is false: hyperactivation changes the beat from wave-like to whip-like. It leaves out 1, which is true: cholesterol and other sterols leave the membrane, making it more fluid.

stem: Where does fertilization most often take place?
choices: The ovary's surface, at the ruptured follicle
ex: The fimbriae at the distal end of the tube capture the oocyte when the follicle ruptures, and fertilization most often happens in the distal fallopian tube, where about 50 sperm arrive. The embryo reaches the uterine cavity days later.
why: Fertilization most often happens in the distal fallopian tube, near the fimbriae that captured the oocyte.
The embryo reaches the uterine cavity about 4 days after ovulation, as a blastocyst.
The cervix is a passage for sperm; its mucus can help or block them.
The fimbriae carry the oocyte from the ovary into the tube; fertilization happens in the tube.

stem: What moves the oocyte along the fallopian tube?
choices: Beating cilia and peristaltic contractions of the tube
The oocyte's own flagellum, once the cumulus is shed
The current of cervical mucus flowing up from the vagina
Sperm that bind the zona pellucida and tow it along
ex: His slide: a combination of beating cilia and peristaltic contractions propels the oocyte, after the fimbriae capture it. His notes add that the contractions respond to estrogen.
why: Cilia and peristaltic contractions together propel the oocyte down the tube.
An oocyte has no flagellum; that is a sperm's tail.
Mucus doesn't carry the oocyte; estrogen thins the mucus so sperm can swim up through it.
Sperm bind the zona to fertilize the oocyte, not to move it.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Just after ovulation, estrogen relaxes the opening of the uterus so the embryo can enter early.
2. When progesterone rises, the myometrium relaxes and the blastocyst can move into the uterus.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Estrogen, still high just after midcycle, promotes constriction of the opening of the uterus where the tube meets it, holding the embryo back while the endometrium gets ready. Rising progesterone relaxes the myometrium, and the blastocyst moves into the uterus.
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: estrogen constricts the opening of the uterus, holding the embryo back while the endometrium gets ready.
Statement 2 is true, not false: rising progesterone relaxes the myometrium, letting the blastocyst into the uterus.

Statement 1 is false, not true: estrogen constricts the opening of the uterus, holding the embryo back while the endometrium gets ready. Statement 2 is true, not false: rising progesterone relaxes the myometrium, letting the blastocyst into the uterus.

Statement 1 is false: estrogen constricts the opening of the uterus, holding the embryo back while the endometrium gets ready. Statement 2 is true: rising progesterone relaxes the myometrium, letting the blastocyst into the uterus.

stem:
Which statements about the timing of early pregnancy are true?
1. Fertilization takes place within 24 hours of ovulation.
2. The blastocyst enters the uterine cavity about 4 days after ovulation.
3. Implantation happens about 5 to 7 days after ovulation.
4. The trophoblasts begin secreting hCG about 2 days after ovulation.
ex: His slides: fertilization within 24 hours of ovulation, the blastocyst (about 100 cells) in the uterine cavity about 4 days after ovulation, implantation 5 to 7 days after ovulation, and hCG from the trophoblasts about 8 days after ovulation. He stressed that these are ranges.
why: It leaves out 3, which is true: implantation happens about 5 to 7 days after ovulation.
Statements 1, 2 and 3 are true. Statement 4 is false: the trophoblasts begin secreting hCG about 8 days after ovulation, after implantation, not 2 days.
It includes 4, which is false: hCG secretion begins about 8 days after ovulation, not 2.
It includes 4, which is false: hCG secretion begins about 8 days after ovulation, not 2. It leaves out 1, which is true: fertilization takes place within 24 hours of ovulation.

stem: At which stage does the embryo implant, and which cells make up its outer layer?
ex: Implantation happens at the blastocyst stage: many cells around a fluid-filled cavity. Its outer layer is made of trophoblasts, which bind to and invade the endometrium and go on to help form the placenta.
why: He said implantation typically happens at the blastocyst stage, and its outer layer is the trophoblasts.
The zygote is the single cell right after fertilization; decidual cells are the mother's endometrial cells.
Myoepithelial cells are in the breast; they contract under oxytocin to let milk down.
The zygote doesn't implant; granulosa cells form the cumulus around the ovulated oocyte.

likely.t: Implantation at the blastocyst stage: trophoblasts, cytotrophoblasts (nurse cells) versus syncytiotrophoblasts (invasion)

stem: Which substances does the blastocyst secrete to help it implant?
choices: Dopamine, oxytocin and prolactin releasing factor
ex: His implantation slide: the blastocyst secretes adhesion molecules (to bind the endometrium), proteases (to break down the matrix and invade) and hormones, chiefly hCG. The uterus answers with decidualization.
why: Adhesion molecules bind the wall, proteases let it invade, and hCG rescues the corpus luteum.
Those are the hypothalamic and pituitary signals of lactation, not the blastocyst's.
Cortical granules and the ZP proteins belong to the oocyte at fertilization.
Relaxin comes from the corpus luteum and placenta, and aromatase and DHEA sulfate belong to estriol synthesis later in pregnancy.

stem: Decidualization makes the endometrium more receptive to the blastocyst. It includes each of the following EXCEPT:
choices: A stronger local immune response against the blastocyst
Increased glycogen stored in vacuoles around the implantation site
Endometrial cells enlarging into decidual cells
ex: Decidualization is a set of changes: increased vascularity, increased glycogen, and immune modulation, a local suppression that keeps the immune system from attacking the blastocyst as foreign. With progesterone, the blastocyst's paracrine factors make the endometrial cells enlarge into decidual cells.
why: The opposite: immune modulation suppresses the local immune response so the blastocyst isn't attacked as foreign.
Increased vascularity is one of the decidual changes on his slide.
More glycogen, stored in vacuoles around the implanting blastocyst, is one of the decidual changes.
Endometrial cells enlarge, store glycogen and become decidual cells, which nourish the embryo until the placenta forms.

stem: When the blastocyst attaches, its trophoblasts split into two populations. Which cells invade the endometrium?
choices: Cytotrophoblasts, the nurse cells that support the embryo
Decidual cells, which digest their own matrix
ex: Attachment signals the trophoblasts to differentiate. Cytotrophoblasts are the nurse cells, nourishing the early embryo and giving it structure. Syncytiotrophoblasts invade: they send out long protrusions that secrete proteases to break down the matrix, and they also make hCG and human placental lactogen.
why: He said the syncytiotrophoblasts are the ones that invade, secreting proteases to burrow into the endometrial lining.
The cytotrophoblasts are the nurse cells; the protease-secreting invaders are the syncytiotrophoblasts.
That describes the cytotrophoblasts correctly, but they nurse the embryo rather than invade.
Decidual cells are the mother's endometrial cells; they nourish the embryo rather than invade.

likely.t: Implantation at the blastocyst stage: trophoblasts, cytotrophoblasts (nurse cells) versus syncytiotrophoblasts (invasion)

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Human placental lactogen is made by the cytotrophoblasts.
2. Human placental lactogen affects the growth and development of breast tissue.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: The syncytiotrophoblasts are the endocrine trophoblasts, making hCG and human placental lactogen; the cytotrophoblasts are the nurse cells. hPL helps breast tissue grow and develop, and it has anti-insulin actions.
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: the syncytiotrophoblasts make hPL; the cytotrophoblasts are the nurse cells.
Statement 2 is true, not false: he said hPL helps with the growth and development of breast tissue.

Statement 1 is false, not true: the syncytiotrophoblasts make hPL; the cytotrophoblasts are the nurse cells. Statement 2 is true, not false: he said hPL helps with the growth and development of breast tissue.
Statement 1 is false: the syncytiotrophoblasts make hPL; the cytotrophoblasts are the nurse cells. Statement 2 is true: he said hPL helps with the growth and development of breast tissue.

stem: Dr. Madison called hCG "the important part" of early pregnancy. What does it do?
choices: Keeps the corpus luteum from regressing, so progesterone and estrogen stay high
Turns the corpus luteum into the corpus albicans, so the placenta can take over early
Relaxes the myometrium so the blastocyst can enter the uterus
Antagonizes prolactin in the breast so milk isn't made until delivery
ex: hCG from the trophoblasts "informs" the corpus luteum that fertilization has occurred and rescues it from regression. The corpus luteum keeps making progesterone and estrogen, in fact more of them, so there is no abrupt loss of the steroids and no menses.
why: "This is what rescues the corpus luteum": without hCG it would regress about 14 days after ovulation.
That is what happens without hCG; hCG prevents the regression into the corpus albicans.
Rising progesterone relaxes the myometrium; hCG's job is the corpus luteum.
Progesterone is the hormone that antagonizes prolactin during pregnancy.

likely.t: hCG rescues the corpus luteum: made by the trophoblasts, it keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone (the hormone that readies the endometrium) and estrogen through the first trimester, LH and FSH stay suppressed, and it is what a pregnancy test measures

stem: Which statement about hCG is false?
choices: It is made by the corpus luteum, which uses it to keep itself from regressing
Under its direction, the corpus luteum makes more progesterone and estrogen
Its levels are highest toward the end of the first trimester, then decline
It can weakly stimulate the TSH receptor, causing a transient gestational hyperthyroidism
ex: hCG is secreted by the trophoblasts (later the placenta), not the corpus luteum. It acts on the corpus luteum, preventing its regression and increasing its progesterone and estrogen. It peaks toward the end of the first trimester, about 10 weeks, and its weak action at the TSH receptor can cause a transient gestational hyperthyroidism.
why: This is the false one: hCG comes from the trophoblasts of the blastocyst; the corpus luteum is its target, not its source.
This is true: under hCG's direction the corpus luteum increases its synthesis of progesterone and estrogen.
This is true: his slide notes put the peak at about 10 weeks, the end of the first trimester, with a decline after.
This is true: his slide notes say hCG binds the TSH receptor weakly, which can cause a transient gestational hyperthyroidism.

likely.t: hCG rescues the corpus luteum: made by the trophoblasts, it keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone (the hormone that readies the endometrium) and estrogen through the first trimester, LH and FSH stay suppressed, and it is what a pregnancy test measures

stem: During the first trimester, which structure makes most of the mother's progesterone and estrogen?
choices: The corpus luteum, kept going by hCG
The placenta, fully formed by implantation
The fetal adrenal glands and liver
ex: The corpus luteum, rescued by hCG, stays intact and makes most of the progesterone and estrogen during the first trimester. The placenta begins developing after implantation and is fully developed by the end of the first trimester; then it takes over the hormone production.
why: He said the corpus luteum is responsible for most of the progesterone and estrogen in the first trimester.
The placenta isn't fully developed until the end of the first trimester; it takes over after that.
The fetal adrenal and liver help the placenta make estriol, but they aren't the main source in the first trimester.
The anterior pituitary makes LH and FSH, which are suppressed in pregnancy; it doesn't make sex steroids.

likely.t: hCG rescues the corpus luteum: made by the trophoblasts, it keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone (the hormone that readies the endometrium) and estrogen through the first trimester, LH and FSH stay suppressed, and it is what a pregnancy test measures

stem: True or false: During pregnancy, release of LH and FSH from the mother's anterior pituitary is suppressed, so the cyclic pattern of the menstrual cycle stops.
ex: The cyclic LH and FSH waves of a normal cycle are shut down in pregnancy, so progesterone and estrogen stay consistently high; it is the secondary amenorrhea of pregnancy. He credited hCG ("slows production of LH and FSH"); textbooks credit the high estrogen and progesterone that hCG maintains.
why: LH and FSH are held down in pregnancy, so their cyclic waves stop and progesterone and estrogen stay consistently high.
The statement is true: LH and FSH are suppressed, which is why periods stop in pregnancy.

likely.t: hCG rescues the corpus luteum: made by the trophoblasts, it keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone (the hormone that readies the endometrium) and estrogen through the first trimester, LH and FSH stay suppressed, and it is what a pregnancy test measures

stem: True or false: A pregnancy test measures hCG, which appears in urine or blood about 10 to 11 days after fertilization.
ex: "It's also what we measure when we do pregnancy tests": hCG rises high, very quickly. His slide notes say it is found in urine or blood around 10 to 11 days after fertilization and peaks at about 10 weeks.
why: He said hCG is what pregnancy tests measure, since it rises high and fast; his notes give 10 to 11 days after fertilization.
Both parts are right: the test measures hCG, detectable about 10 to 11 days after fertilization.

likely.t: hCG rescues the corpus luteum: made by the trophoblasts, it keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone (the hormone that readies the endometrium) and estrogen through the first trimester, LH and FSH stay suppressed, and it is what a pregnancy test measures

stem: Which explanation from Dr. Madison's slides best fits her thyroid labs?
choices: hCG weakly stimulates the TSH receptor, and estrogen raises TBG, so total T4 rises more than free T4
Human placental lactogen stimulates her thyroid directly, so free T4 has doubled while total T4 barely moved
Estrogen lowers TBG, so more T4 circulates free and suppresses her TSH
Relaxin from the corpus luteum blocks TSH release from the anterior pituitary
ex: His hCG slide notes: hCG can bind the TSH receptor weakly, causing a transient gestational hyperthyroidism, most likely near the hCG peak at about 10 weeks. Estrogen also raises thyroid-binding globulin (TBG), so total T3 and T4 can double while free T3 and T4 don't rise dramatically.
pbox: Nausea; feels warm and a little jittery
No thyroid disease before this pregnancy; no goiter
TSH 0.2 mIU/L (reference 0.4 to 4.0); total T4 15 mcg/dL (reference 5 to 12); free T4 1.6 ng/dL (reference 0.8 to 1.8)
why: hCG's weak TSH-receptor action suppresses her TSH, and the extra TBG from estrogen raises total T4 while free T4 stays near normal.
hPL acts on the breast and opposes insulin; it isn't a thyroid stimulator, and her free T4 is within range.
Estrogen raises TBG rather than lowering it, which is why her total T4 is high while free T4 is normal.
Relaxin quiets the myometrium and softens the cervix; it has no thyroid role in this lecture.

stem: Which statement about the placenta is true?
choices: It starts developing shortly after implantation and is fully developed by the end of the first trimester
It is fully developed at implantation, so it makes most of the progesterone and estrogen from the very first week
It keeps the mother's antibodies from crossing into the fetus
It disposes of the fetus's waste products into the amniotic fluid rather than the mother's blood
ex: The placenta begins developing shortly after implantation and is fully developed by the end of the first trimester, when it takes over hormone production from the corpus luteum. It exchanges gases and nutrients, makes hormones, lets maternal antibodies through while protecting the fetus from many infections, and removes fetal waste into the mother's circulation.
why: This is the true one: the corpus luteum carries the first trimester because the placenta isn't fully developed until its end.
The placenta isn't fully developed until the end of the first trimester; the corpus luteum, rescued by hCG, makes most of the steroids until then.
His slide says the placenta lets maternal antibodies pass through while protecting the fetus from many infections.
Fetal waste goes into the mother's circulation, so she can excrete it.

stem: Which crosses the placenta from the fetus to the mother?
ex: Oxygen, water, electrolytes and nutrients (lipids, amino acids, carbohydrates, vitamins) go from mother to fetus. Carbon dioxide and the fetus's metabolic waste go back to the mother, who excretes them. Hormones and antibodies cross too, and so can some drugs and viruses.
why: The fetus hands carbon dioxide and its metabolic waste to the mother, who excretes them.
Oxygen and water go from mother to fetus.
Nutrients such as amino acids, lipids and carbohydrates go from mother to fetus.
Vitamins and electrolytes go from mother to fetus.

stem: True or false: The placental barrier keeps drugs and viruses from reaching the fetus.
ex: The placenta is a selective barrier that protects the fetus from many infections, but it isn't absolute: he said certain drugs and some viruses can pass from mother to fetus, so be careful about what crosses.
why: He warned that certain drugs and some viruses can pass from mother to fetus.
Some drugs and some viruses do cross, which is why he said to be careful about what goes through.

stem: The placenta produces each of the following hormones EXCEPT:
ex: His placenta slide lists hCG, progesterone, estrogen and human placental lactogen, and relaxin comes from both the placenta and the corpus luteum. Oxytocin comes from the mother's posterior pituitary (made in the hypothalamus).
why: Oxytocin is a posterior pituitary hormone, released during labor and nursing.
Human placental lactogen is a placental hormone: breast growth and anti-insulin actions.
After the first trimester the placenta makes progesterone on its own.
The placenta makes hCG once the trophoblasts have begun it.

likely.t: What the placenta makes: hCG, hPL, relaxin, progesterone and estriol, but not oxytocin

stem: Human placental lactogen is also called what?
ex: He gave both names: human placental lactogen, also called human chorionic somatomammotropin. It helps breast tissue develop and has anti-insulin actions. Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is the hormone that rescues the corpus luteum.
why: Both names belong to the same placental hormone, made by the syncytiotrophoblasts.
hCG is a different hormone: it rescues the corpus luteum and is what pregnancy tests detect.
Prolactin releasing factor is a hypothalamic signal that raises prolactin after delivery.
Relaxin is a separate hormone of the corpus luteum and placenta that keeps the uterus quiet.

stem: Which action of human placental lactogen keeps nutrients flowing to the fetus?
choices: Lipolysis and the breakdown of carbohydrates and proteins
Storing glucose as glycogen in the mother's liver and muscle
Keeping the corpus luteum making progesterone and estrogen
Relaxing the myometrium and the pelvic ligaments
ex: hPL has anti-insulin actions: lipolysis and the breakdown of carbohydrates and proteins, which maintain a continuous flow of nutrients to the fetus. That helps make pregnancy an insulin-resistant, hyperinsulinemic state.
why: hPL opposes insulin: lipolysis and carbohydrate and protein breakdown keep fuel flowing to the fetus.
Storing glucose is insulin's work; hPL opposes insulin and breaks fuels down.
That is hCG's job; hPL acts on the breast and on fuel metabolism.
That is relaxin's job, from the corpus luteum and placenta.

likely.t: Human placental lactogen opposes insulin: an insulin-resistant, hyperinsulinemic pregnancy and gestational diabetes

stem: True or false: Pregnancy is an insulin-resistant state in which the mother's insulin levels fall.
ex: His slides call pregnancy an insulin-resistant, hyperinsulinemic state: anti-insulin hormones such as human placental lactogen blunt the tissues' response to insulin, fat use rises and glucose is spared, and insulin levels can run very high. Some mothers develop gestational diabetes.
why: Pregnancy is insulin resistant and hyperinsulinemic: the tissues respond less, so insulin levels run high.
The statement gets the insulin level backward: it rises, the hyperinsulinemic half of his slide.

likely.t: Human placental lactogen opposes insulin: an insulin-resistant, hyperinsulinemic pregnancy and gestational diabetes

stem: How does Dr. Madison's lecture explain her new hyperglycemia?
choices: Placental hormones such as hPL oppose insulin, so pregnancy is insulin resistant and hyperinsulinemic
hCG triggers an immune attack on her beta cells, so she now makes too little insulin, as in type 1 diabetes
Relaxin blocks the release of insulin from her pancreas during the second trimester
Progesterone antagonizes prolactin, and the rising prolactin drives her glucose up
ex: Pregnancy is an insulin-resistant, hyperinsulinemic state: hormones such as human placental lactogen have anti-insulin actions, her tissues respond less to insulin, her insulin runs high and her glucose rises. He called gestational diabetes multifactorial: largely hormonal, with a genetic predisposition in some mothers, like her family history.
pbox: No diabetes before this pregnancy; her mother has type 2 diabetes
75 g oral glucose tolerance test: fasting 98 mg/dL, 1 hour 192 mg/dL, 2 hours 170 mg/dL
Fasting insulin above the reference range
why: hPL's anti-insulin actions, with other pregnancy hormones, drive insulin resistance with high insulin; her family history adds the genetic side he mentioned.
Her insulin is high, not low, and hCG's job is the corpus luteum; beta-cell destruction is type 1 diabetes.
Relaxin quiets the myometrium and softens the cervix; it doesn't block insulin release.
Progesterone does hold back prolactin's milk-making in the breast, but that isn't why her glucose rises.

likely.t: Human placental lactogen opposes insulin: an insulin-resistant, hyperinsulinemic pregnancy and gestational diabetes

stem: Which statement about relaxin is false?
choices: It stimulates myometrial contractions, which helps start labor early
It is made by the corpus luteum, in response to hCG, and by the placenta
It relaxes the pelvic bones and ligaments and softens the cervix
It keeps the uterus quiet in early pregnancy, helping to prevent a preterm delivery
ex: Relaxin, from the corpus luteum (in response to hCG) and the placenta, inhibits myometrial contractions so the uterus stays quiet in early pregnancy: "the last thing we want is a preterm delivery." It relaxes the pelvic bones and ligaments, softens the cervix, and may help thin the cervix at term.
why: This is the false one: relaxin inhibits myometrial contractions; it keeps the uterus quiet to prevent a preterm delivery.
This is true: his slide names both sources, the corpus luteum (in response to hCG) and the placenta.
This is true: it is on his relaxin slide, and he said it helps thin the cervix at the end of term.
This is true: he said relaxin keeps the myometrium quiescent so contractions don't start labor too early.

stem: Which estrogen predominates during pregnancy?
ex: His three estrogens: estradiol is the estrogen of the normal menstrual cycle, estrone the estrogen of menopause, and estriol the predominant estrogen of pregnancy, made by the placenta with the fetus's help.
why: Estriol is the predominant estrogen during pregnancy.
Estradiol is the estrogen of the normal menstrual cycle.
Estrone is the estrogen of menopause.
16-hydroxy DHEA sulfate is the fetal precursor the placenta converts to estriol, not an estrogen itself.

likely.t: The placenta takes over the steroids: estriol is the estrogen of pregnancy; the placenta makes progesterone on its own but needs the fetal adrenal's 17,20 desmolase and the fetal liver before its aromatase makes estriol

stem: Why does the placenta need the fetus to make estrogen?
choices: It lacks 17,20 desmolase, which the fetal adrenal has
It lacks aromatase, which the fetal liver has
It lacks cholesterol desmolase, so the fetus must make pregnenolone
It lacks cholesterol, which only the fetus can make
ex: The placenta has cholesterol desmolase (cholesterol to pregnenolone) and aromatase, but not 17,20 desmolase, and you need an androgen to make an estrogen. The fetal adrenal supplies that step, making DHEA sulfate; the fetal liver hydroxylates it; and the placenta's aromatase finishes estriol.
why: The fetus has 17,20 desmolase, which the placenta is missing, so the fetal adrenal makes the androgen precursor.
The placenta has aromatase; it does the last step to estriol.
The placenta has cholesterol desmolase; it makes pregnenolone from the mother's cholesterol.
The cholesterol comes from the mother, mostly from her diet.

likely.t: The placenta takes over the steroids: estriol is the estrogen of pregnancy; the placenta makes progesterone on its own but needs the fetal adrenal's 17,20 desmolase and the fetal liver before its aromatase makes estriol

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. The placenta's aromatase converts 16-hydroxy DHEA sulfate from the fetus into estriol.
2. The fetal kidney adds the 16-hydroxyl group to DHEA sulfate before it returns to the placenta.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: The fetal adrenal makes DHEA sulfate (the sulfate prevents virilization of the fetus), the fetal liver hydroxylates it to 16-hydroxy DHEA sulfate, and the placenta's aromatase converts that to estriol. That is why estriol reflects the health of the fetal adrenals and liver.
why: Statement 2 is false, not true: the 16-hydroxylation happens in the fetal liver, not the kidney.
Statement 1 is true, not false: the placenta's aromatase makes estriol from the fetus's 16-hydroxy DHEA sulfate.
Statement 1 is true: the placenta's aromatase makes estriol from the fetus's 16-hydroxy DHEA sulfate. Statement 2 is false: the 16-hydroxylation happens in the fetal liver, not the kidney.

Statement 1 is true, not false: the placenta's aromatase makes estriol from the fetus's 16-hydroxy DHEA sulfate. Statement 2 is false, not true: the 16-hydroxylation happens in the fetal liver, not the kidney.

stem: True or false: The placenta can make estrogen on its own, but it needs the fetus to make progesterone.
ex: The placenta synthesizes progesterone well on its own from the mother's cholesterol. For estrogen it lacks 17,20 desmolase, so the fetal adrenal and liver make the precursor that the placenta's aromatase turns into estriol.
why: It is the other way around: the placenta makes progesterone on its own and needs the fetal adrenal and liver to make estrogen.
The statement swaps the two: progesterone is the placenta's alone; estrogen needs the fetus.

likely.t: The placenta takes over the steroids: estriol is the estrogen of pregnancy; the placenta makes progesterone on its own but needs the fetal adrenal's 17,20 desmolase and the fetal liver before its aromatase makes estriol

stem: Why can the mother's estriol level reflect the health of the fetus?
choices: Making it requires a working fetal adrenal gland and liver
It is made only by the fetal kidneys and excreted into the amniotic fluid
It is made by the mother's ovaries only when fetal hCG is present
It rises only when the fetus is stressed and making cortisol
ex: His slide notes: estriol needs the fetal adrenal (DHEA sulfate) and the fetal liver (16-hydroxylation) before the placenta's aromatase finishes it, so its level reflects healthy fetal adrenal glands and liver. To make estrogen, the placenta "needs help from the baby."
why: Estriol synthesis runs through the fetal adrenal and liver, so a low level can signal a problem with the fetus.
The fetal kidney isn't part of the estriol pathway; the adrenal and liver are.
Estriol is made by the placenta from fetal precursors, not by the mother's ovaries.
Estriol is made all through pregnancy from the fetal adrenal's DHEA sulfate; it isn't a stress signal.

stem: True or false: Parturition occurs about 40 weeks after fertilization.
ex: Parturition, the delivery of the fetus, occurs about 40 weeks after the onset of the last menstrual period, which comes about two weeks before fertilization.
why: His slide counts the 40 weeks from the onset of the last menstrual period, not from fertilization.
The starting point is wrong: it is about 40 weeks after the onset of the last menstrual period.

stem:
Which statements about the start of labor are true?
1. Distention of the uterus by the growing fetus is one trigger.
2. The uterus makes fewer receptors for PGF2 alpha and oxytocin.
3. Prostaglandins raise intracellular calcium in the myometrium.
4. Oxytocin and the prostaglandins act synergistically.
ex: His slide: distention of the uterus, upregulation of uterine receptors for PGF2 alpha and oxytocin, more uterine sensitivity to estrogen and less to progesterone, more prostaglandins (which raise intracellular calcium and soften the cervix), and more oxytocin from the posterior pituitary, which synergizes with the prostaglandins.
why: It includes 2, which is false: receptors for PGF2 alpha and oxytocin are upregulated, not reduced. It leaves out 4, which is true: oxytocin synergizes with the prostaglandins.
Statements 1, 3 and 4 are true. Statement 2 is false: the uterus upregulates its receptors for PGF2 alpha and oxytocin.
It leaves out 3, which is true: prostaglandins raise intracellular calcium, so contractions get stronger.
It leaves out 1, which is true: the fetus grows so large it stretches the uterus, a mechanical trigger.

likely.t: Delivery and after: the estrogen-to-progesterone ratio rises; uterine distention, prostaglandins (PGF2 alpha for contraction, PGE2 for the cervix) and oxytocin from the posterior pituitary drive labor; oxytocin limits bleeding after delivery

stem: Near term, how does the balance of estrogen and progesterone change, and what does that do to the myometrium?

The spleen's trabeculae contain myofibroblasts, but its stroma is reticular fibers and cells, like the other organs'.
A lymph node's stroma is reticular fibers and cells; follicular dendritic cells sit among the B cells of the germinal centers.

likely.t: The thymus: epithelioreticular cells form its stroma ("I do want you to know that"), reticular cells everywhere else; the dense, dark cortex versus the lighter medulla; and involution to fat by the teens

stem: True or false: B cells and NK cells form and mature in the bone marrow, while T cell precursors leave the marrow immunoincompetent and mature in the thymus.
ex: B and NK cells are formed and mature in the bone marrow, then enter the blood and populate the secondary organs, epithelia and connective tissue. T cell precursors originate in the marrow, leave it immunoincompetent, travel to the thymus, and mature there as CD4-positive or CD8-positive cells. His summary: bone marrow, B cells; thymus, T cells.
why: B and NK cells mature in the marrow; T cell precursors start there but finish in the thymus.
The statement is true: T cell precursors leave the marrow immunoincompetent and mature in the thymus, while B and NK cells mature in the marrow.

likely.t: Primary versus secondary lymphoid organs: the primary ones are just the bone marrow and the thymus (not GALT), where B and T cells become immunocompetent without antigen ("bone marrow, B cells, thymus, T cells"); every other one, lymph nodes, MALT and GALT, and the spleen, is secondary

stem: Where are self-reactive B cells eliminated?
choices: In the germinal centers of lymph nodes
In the marginal zone of the spleen
ex: In the marrow, stromal cells interact with B cells and make the cytokines that govern their development; self-reactive B cells are eliminated, and the immunocompetent ones, each with one antigen-specific IgM or IgD, travel to the secondary organs.
why: B cells develop in the marrow, guided by the stromal cells' cytokines, and the self-reactive ones are eliminated there before the rest leave.
The thymic medulla is where negative selection removes self-reactive T cells.
Germinal centers are where B cells proliferate after meeting antigen.
The marginal zone holds macrophages and some B cells around the white pulp; it isn't where B cells are screened.

stem: Which statement about the thymus is false?
choices: Its capsule and trabeculae carry both afferent and efferent lymphatic vessels
It lies behind the manubrium, in the superior and anterior mediastinum
Its T cell receptors gain their antigenic diversity by gene rearrangement
Its epithelioreticular cells come from endoderm, and its capsule from mesoderm
ex: The thymus is a flattened, bilobed organ behind the manubrium. Its capsule and trabeculae carry blood vessels, nerves and efferent (not afferent) lymphatics. Pharyngeal pouch endoderm gives its epithelioreticular cells and mesoderm its capsule and trabeculae, and gene rearrangement there gives the T cell receptors their diversity.
why: This is the false one: the thymus has efferent but not afferent lymphatics; only the lymph node has both.
This is true: it lies behind the manubrium and extends into the superior and anterior mediastinum.
This is true: gene rearrangement in the thymus generates the T cell receptors' antigenic diversity.
This is true: pharyngeal pouch endoderm gives the epithelioreticular cells, and mesoderm the capsule and trabeculae.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. The thymic cortex stains darker than the medulla because its developing T cells are densely packed.
2. Hassall's corpuscles, concentric layers of flattened epithelial cells, are found in the thymic medulla.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Cortex: densely packed developing T cells hide the epithelioreticular cells, so it stains darker, and macrophages remove the cells that fail. Medulla: more epithelioreticular cells, loosely packed bigger T cells, lighter staining, and Hassall's corpuscles.
why: Statement 1 is true: the cortex is crowded with small developing T cells, so it stains darker. Statement 2 is true: Hassall's corpuscles are the distinguishing feature of the medulla.

Statement 1 is true, not false: the cortex is crowded with small developing T cells, so it stains darker. Statement 2 is true, not false: Hassall's corpuscles are the distinguishing feature of the medulla.
Statement 2 is true, not false: Hassall's corpuscles are the distinguishing feature of the medulla.

stem:
Which are parts of the blood-thymus barrier?
1. The capillary endothelium and its basement membrane
2. Follicular dendritic cells holding antigen-antibody complexes
3. The perivascular connective tissue, with its macrophages
4. Epithelioreticular cells
ex: He listed the blood-thymus barrier's three layers: an epithelioreticular cell layer, a perivascular connective tissue layer (with macrophages, his slide adds) and the capillary wall, its endothelium and basement membrane. It protects the developing T cells from antigens in the blood.
why: It includes 2, which is false: follicular dendritic cells sit in the germinal centers of lymph nodes, not the thymus. It leaves out 3, which is true: the perivascular connective tissue, with its macrophages, is the barrier's middle layer.
It leaves out 4, which is true: the epithelioreticular cells are the barrier's outer layer.
Statements 1, 3 and 4 are true. Statement 2 is false: follicular dendritic cells sit in the germinal centers of lymph nodes, not the thymus.

It includes 2, which is false: follicular dendritic cells sit in the germinal centers of lymph nodes, not the thymus. It leaves out 1, which is true: the capillary endothelium and its basement membrane are the barrier's inner layer.

stem:
Which statements about T cell education in the thymus are true?
1. T cell precursors enter the thymus through postcapillary venules.
2. Positive selection takes place in the thymic cortex.
3. Negative selection removes T cells aimed at self antigen displayed on self MHC.
4. The survivors leave the thymus positive for both CD4 and CD8.
ex: Precursors, negative for CD4 and CD8, enter through postcapillary venules and migrate to the cortex, gain the T cell receptor, CD3, CD4 and CD8, pass positive selection in the cortex and negative selection in the medulla, and leave as CD4-positive or CD8-positive cells.
why: It leaves out 3, which is true: negative selection, in the medulla, eliminates the cells directed at self antigen on self MHC.
Statements 1, 2 and 3 are true. Statement 4 is false: survivors leave as single-positive cells, either CD4-positive helper or CD8-positive cytotoxic T cells.
It includes 4, which is false: survivors leave as either CD4-positive or CD8-positive cells, not both. It leaves out 2, which is true: positive selection happens in the cortex.
It includes 4, which is false: survivors leave as either CD4-positive or CD8-positive cells, not both. It leaves out 1, which is true: precursors enter through postcapillary venules.

likely.t: T cell education: precursors in through postcapillary venules, out to the cortex, positive and negative selection, single CD4 or CD8 cells out to the secondary organs, and 95 to 99 percent selected out by apoptosis

stem: True or false: About 95 to 99 percent of thymocytes die by apoptosis in the thymus during selection.
ex: Selection is strict: about 95 to 99 percent of thymocytes undergo apoptosis, and macrophages in the cortex phagocytose the T cells that fail their thymic education.
why: Most thymocytes fail selection and die by apoptosis, and the cortex's macrophages clear them.
The statement is true: only a small fraction of thymocytes survive selection.

likely.t: T cell education: precursors in through postcapillary venules, out to the cortex, positive and negative selection, single CD4 or CD8 cells out to the secondary organs, and 95 to 99 percent selected out by apoptosis

stem: What best explains the fat where his thymus should be?
choices: Normal involution: from the early teens, fat replaces the thymus
A failed blood-thymus barrier, letting antigens destroy the gland
Fat cells normally fill the thymus at every age, so it always looks this way
An enlarged, overactive thymus, which peaks in middle age
ex: He said the thymus is very large when you're born and little, then by the teens, or a little past, it involutes and fat replaces it: in a donor you see a lot of fat in front of the heart, where the old thymus was. His slide gives about 12 to 15 grams at birth and 30 to 40 grams by puberty.
pbox: 58-year-old man, chest CT for an unrelated reason
Fat in the anterior mediastinum behind the manubrium, where the thymus lies; no mass
why: The thymus is largest and most active in the newborn and before adolescence, then involutes from the early teens as adipose tissue replaces it.
The barrier protects developing T cells from antigens; its failure isn't what turns the thymus to fat.
The thymus is largest and most active in newborns and children; fat replaces it only after involution begins.
The thymus peaks before adolescence (about 30 to 40 grams by puberty), not in middle age.

likely.t: The thymus: epithelioreticular cells form its stroma ("I do want you to know that"), reticular cells everywhere else; the dense, dark cortex versus the lighter medulla; and involution to fat by the teens

stem:
Which pairings of a region and the lymphocytes that fill it are correct?
1. Lymph node paracortex: mainly B cells
2. Lymph node cortical follicles: mainly B cells
3. Interfollicular regions of Peyer's patches: mainly T cells
4. MALT nodules: mainly B cells
ex: B cells: the lymph node's cortical follicles, the spleen's nodules, MALT's nodules. T cells: the lymph node's paracortex, the spleen's PALS, and the areas around MALT's nodules (the interfollicular regions of Peyer's patches).
why: It includes 1, which is false: the paracortex is the lymph node's T cell zone. It leaves out 4, which is true: B cells dominate MALT's nodules.
It includes 1, which is false: the paracortex is the lymph node's T cell zone. It leaves out 2, which is true: the cortex's follicles are B cells.
It leaves out 4, which is true: B cells dominate MALT's nodules, with T cells in the areas around them.
Statements 2, 3 and 4 are true. Statement 1 is false: the paracortex is the lymph node's T cell zone; the B cells are in the cortex's follicles.

stem: In the spleen's white pulp, which cells make up the periarteriolar lymphatic sheath (PALS) around the central arteriole?
ex: He said the PALS, the periarteriolar lymphatic sheath around the central artery of the white pulp, is "associated with the T-cell area." B cells are in the nodules farther out, and a marginal zone with macrophages and some B cells surrounds the white pulp.
why: T cells gather in the PALS around the central arteriole; the B cell nodules lie farther out in the white pulp.
B cells are in the white pulp's nodules, which sit to one side and push the arteriole off center.
Macrophages sit in the marginal zone and the red pulp's cords; the PALS is a cuff of lymphocytes.
Erythrocytes give the red pulp its color; the PALS is white pulp.

likely.t: The spleen: the PALS, the T cell sheath around the central artery ("associate this PALS with the spleen"); white pulp and red pulp; and what the spleen does

stem: What surrounds the spleen's white pulp, and what does it contain?
choices: The marginal zone: macrophages and some B cells
The PALS: T cells wrapped around a central arteriole
The splenic cords: reticular fibers and every kind of blood cell
The mantle zone: small lymphocytes around a germinal center
ex: Around the white pulp is a shell of sparsely cellular lymphoid tissue, the marginal zone, with macrophages and some B cells, supplied by the marginal sinuses. The PALS is inside the white pulp, and the cords are red pulp.
why: A shell of sparsely cellular tissue, the marginal zone, surrounds the white pulp, with macrophages and some B cells; the marginal sinuses supply it.

The splenic cords are red pulp, between the sinuses.

stem: What makes up the spleen's red pulp?
ex: Red pulp, most of the spleen and colored by its red cells, is venous sinusoids and the splenic cords (cords of Billroth) between them. The cords hold a reticular scaffold with reticular cells, lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages and all the formed elements of the blood.
why: Red pulp is thin-walled venous sinusoids with the splenic cords (of Billroth) between them.
Nodules with germinal centers are the B cell part of the white pulp.
The PALS is white pulp: T cells around the central arterioles.
Those are the features of the thymic medulla.

stem: True or false: The spleen's parenchyma, the splenic pulp, comes in two kinds: white pulp and red pulp.
ex: He said the spleen's parenchyma is called the splenic pulp, and it can be white pulp or red pulp. White pulp is lymphoid tissue around a central arteriole, with the PALS; red pulp is the splenic cords and the sinuses between them.
why: The splenic pulp is white pulp (lymphoid tissue around central arterioles, with the PALS) and red pulp (the splenic cords and sinuses), named for their colors in the fresh spleen.
The statement is true: he said the splenic pulp can be either white pulp or red pulp.

likely.t: The spleen: the PALS, the T cell sheath around the central artery ("associate this PALS with the spleen"); white pulp and red pulp; and what the spleen does

stem: True or false: The spleen has efferent lymphatic vessels at its hilum but no afferent lymphatics.
ex: The splenic artery brings in blood-borne antigens and lymphocytes; the splenic vein and the lymphatics leave at the hilum. The spleen filters blood, and it lacks afferent lymphatics.
why: Blood-borne antigens arrive by the splenic artery; lymphatics only leave, at the hilum.
The statement is true: the spleen filters blood, not lymph, and has no afferent lymphatics.

stem: Each of the following is a job of the spleen EXCEPT:
choices: Educating T cells before they meet any antigen
Removing aged and defective red cells and platelets
Storing about a third of the body's platelets
Recycling iron from red blood cells
ex: The spleen filters blood (particulate matter, infectious microorganisms, aged and defective red cells and platelets), recycles iron, stores about a third of the platelets, and responds to blood-borne antigens, making lymphocytes, plasma cells, IgM and IgG.
why: That is the thymus's job; the spleen is a secondary organ, where T and B cells are activated by blood-borne antigens.
The spleen clears particulate matter, infectious microorganisms, and aged and defective red cells and platelets.
His notes say the spleen stores about a third of the body's platelets.
The spleen recycles iron from the red cells it removes.

likely.t: The spleen: the PALS, the T cell sheath around the central artery ("associate this PALS with the spleen"); white pulp and red pulp; and what the spleen does

stem: In the spleen's open circulation, where do the sheathed capillaries empty?
choices: Into the open meshwork of the splenic cords
Straight into the endothelium-lined splenic sinuses
Into the marginal sinuses around the white pulp
Into the trabecular veins, bypassing the red pulp
ex: Splenic artery, trabecular arteries, central arterioles in the white pulp (with their PALS), then straight penicillar arterioles into the red pulp and sheathed capillaries wrapped in macrophages. In the open circulation they empty into the cords; macrophages sample the blood, and it squeezes back into the sinuses, then the trabecular veins and the splenic vein.
why: In the open circulation, sheathed capillaries empty into the reticular meshwork of the cords, where macrophages sample the blood before it reenters through the sinuses.
Emptying straight into the sinuses is the closed route; the open circulation is defined by not doing so.
Marginal sinuses are fed by other branches of the central arteriole, and they supply the marginal zone.
The trabecular veins come after the sinuses, carrying blood to the splenic vein.

stem: How do blood cells get from the splenic cords back into the sinuses?
choices: They squeeze through slits between rod-shaped endothelial cells
They pass through pores in the sinus's thick, continuous basal lamina
They are carried across a smooth muscle wall by pericytes
They enter through the efferent lymphatic vessels at the hilum
ex: Splenic sinuses: rod-shaped, loosely packed endothelial cells running lengthwise with slits between them, strands of basal lamina looping at right angles around them (hoops on a leaky barrel), no smooth muscle, no pericytes, and macrophage processes reaching between the cells to monitor the blood.
why: The sinus wall is loosely packed, rod-shaped endothelial cells with slit-like spaces between them, and the blood cells squeeze through.
The sinus has only strands of basal lamina, looping around the endothelial cells like hoops on a leaky barrel.
Splenic sinuses have no smooth muscle and no pericytes.
Efferent lymphatics carry lymph out of the spleen; blood cells return to the circulation through the sinuses.

stem:

2. White pulp makes up most of the spleen's volume.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: The spleen is the largest lymphoid organ in adults, about the size of a clenched fist, in the upper left quadrant behind the stomach. Most of it is red pulp, sinusoids and cords full of red cells; the white pulp is islands of lymphoid tissue around central arterioles.
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: in adults the spleen is the largest lymphoid organ, about the size of a clenched fist. Statement 2 is false, not true: red pulp makes up most of the spleen.
Statement 1 is false: in adults the spleen is the largest lymphoid organ, about the size of a clenched fist. Statement 2 is false: red pulp makes up most of the spleen.

stem: True or false: Like blood capillaries, lymphatic capillaries rest on a basal lamina.
ex: Lymphatic vessels begin as blind-ended capillaries in loose connective tissue. Their walls are permeable, so large molecules, antigens and cells enter; they lack a basal lamina, and anchoring filaments tie them to nearby collagen so they don't collapse. They join into the thoracic duct, and the large lymphatics drain into the subclavian veins.
why: Lymphatic capillaries are built like blood capillaries except that they lack a basal lamina, which is part of why their walls are so permeable.
The statement is false: lymphatic capillaries lack a basal lamina; anchoring filaments hold them open instead.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. The lymph node is the only lymphoid structure with both afferent and efferent lymphatic vessels.
2. A primary (unstimulated) follicle has a germinal center surrounded by a mantle zone.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true

A primary follicle is a spherical aggregate of B cells; after antigenic stimulation it becomes a secondary follicle with a germinal center (B cell proliferation) inside a mantle zone of small lymphocytes.
why: Statement 2 is false, not true: the germinal center and mantle zone mark a secondary follicle, which forms after antigenic stimulation.

stem: Lymphocytes arriving in a lymph node from the blood cross into its deep cortex through which vessels?
ex: Blood enters the node through an artery at the hilum, and its lymphocytes cross high endothelial venules (HEVs) into the deep cortex; T cells go to the paracortex and B cells to the cortex. Lymph comes in by the afferent lymphatics, and both leave by the efferent lymphatic.

stem: Why are follicular dendritic cells not antigen-presenting cells?
choices: They lack MHC class II molecules
They have no Fc receptors to hold antigen
They live in the paracortex, away from B cells
They destroy antigen by phagocytosis first
ex: A lymph node's supporting cells: reticular cells make the type III collagen and matrix of the stroma; dendritic cells present antigen to T cells; macrophages phagocytose and present (fewer than dendritic cells); follicular dendritic cells interdigitate between B cells in germinal centers and hold antigen-antibody complexes by Fc receptors, but lack MHC II.
why: Follicular dendritic cells hold antigen-antibody complexes on their processes but lack MHC II, so they present nothing.
They do have Fc receptors: that is how antigen-antibody complexes stick to their processes.
They sit in the germinal centers, their thin processes between the B cells; the paracortex is the T cell zone.
Phagocytosis is the macrophage's job; follicular dendritic cells hold antigen on their surface.

stem: Each of the following is a job of the lymph nodes EXCEPT:
choices: Removing aged red blood cells from the blood
Filtering the lymph before it reaches the thoracic duct
Producing lymphocytes that are added to the lymph
ex: Lymph nodes filter lymph before it returns to the thoracic duct, produce lymphocytes that are added to the lymph, make antibodies (mostly IgG) and recirculate lymphocytes. Filtering blood, and clearing its aged red cells, is the spleen's job.
why: Removing aged red cells is the spleen's job; the lymph node filters lymph, not blood.
Lymph percolates through the nodes, which filter it before it returns to the thoracic duct.
Nodes produce lymphocytes and add them to the lymph.
Nodes synthesize antibodies, predominantly IgG.

stem: How did antigens from her infection reach the node, and where in it will her B cells multiply?
choices: In the afferent lymph; in germinal centers of the cortex's follicles
In the blood, crossing the high endothelial venules; in the medulla's sinuses
In the efferent lymphatic; in the paracortex around the venules
Through the splenic artery; in the PALS of the white pulp
ex: Lymph from the infected area reaches the regional node through the afferent lymphatics, carrying antigen in soluble form or on dendritic cells. B cells meet the antigen and helper T cells, and germinal centers develop in the cortex's follicles as the B cells proliferate and differentiate; plasma cells release antibody into the lymph. That growth is why the node swells.
pbox: Toothache and swelling at a lower left first molar for 4 days
Periapical radiolucency at the molar; a tender, enlarged submandibular lymph node, about 1.5 cm
why: Antigen enters through the lymphatic vessels, carried by dendritic cells or in soluble form; after meeting antigen and T cells, B cells form germinal centers in the cortex's follicles.
High endothelial venules let lymphocytes in from the blood; antigen from the tissues arrives in the lymph, and B cells multiply in the cortex.
The efferent lymphatic carries lymph out of the node, and the paracortex is the T cell zone.
The splenic artery and the PALS belong to the spleen, which filters blood.

likely.t: The lymph node: the lymph's route (afferent lymphatic, subcapsular sinus, trabecular sinuses, efferent lymphatic); activation in the paracortex and follicles, B cells multiplying in germinal centers and plasma cells secreting antibody in the medulla

stem: What do the M cells over the Peyer's patches do?

Make IgA and secrete it into the lumen of the ileum
Present antigen on MHC I to cytotoxic T cells in the lumen
Form the germinal centers where the patch's B cells multiply

why: M cells take up microorganisms and macromolecules by endocytosis and release them at their basolateral side, near B cells and CD4-positive T cells.
IgA is made by plasma cells in MALT and actively transported into the lumen; M cells carry antigen the other way.
M cells are antigen-transporting epithelial cells; they don't present antigen to T cells.
Germinal centers form in the nodules under the epithelium, from B cells.

stem: Where are the Peyer's patches?
choices: In the wall of the ileum
In the wall of the stomach
In the lamina propria of the esophagus
At the base of the tongue
ex: Peyer's patches are numerous aggregates of lymphoid nodules in the ileum, part of GALT, covered by the antigen-transporting M cells. GALT also includes the tonsils and the appendix.

The esophagus has scattered MALT, but the Peyer's patches are in the ileum.

stem: Which antibody is the main one made in MALT and actively transported into the mucosal lumen?
ex: MALT is diffuse lymphocytes and unencapsulated nodules in the lamina propria of the GI, respiratory and genitourinary tracts (GALT, BALT, NALT, VALT). Its secondary nodules make plasma cells, and its main antibody is IgA, actively transported into the mucosal lumen.
why: IgA is MALT's main antibody, actively transported into the lumen.

stem: Which tonsils make up Waldeyer's ring?
choices: Palatine, lingual and the Peyer's patches of the ileum
The pharyngeal and tubal tonsils of the nasopharynx only

stem: What is this condition called?
choices: Adenoiditis: an enlarged, inflamed pharyngeal tonsil
Palatine tonsillitis: inflamed tonsils in the oropharynx wall
Lingual tonsil enlargement at the base of the tongue
Thymic enlargement in the anterior mediastinum

Mouth breathing at rest; palatine tonsils a normal size; his physician's note describes an enlarged, chronically inflamed lymphoid mass in the back of the nasopharynx

stem: Which blood cells are fragments of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow, and what is their main job?
choices: Erythrocytes, which carry oxygen and carbon dioxide
Neutrophils, which engulf and kill bacteria
Monocytes, which become the macrophages in the tissues
ex: Blood holds three kinds of cells: the erythrocytes, about 99 percent of the cells, carry oxygen and carbon dioxide; the platelets, fragments of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow, initiate blood clotting; and the white cells defend the body.
why: Platelets are fragments of megakaryocytes, made in the bone marrow, and they initiate blood clotting.

likely.t: Recognizing the blood cells and their jobs: red cells (most of the cells) carry oxygen and carbon dioxide, platelets come from megakaryocytes ("just knowledge you should know") and start clotting, and the white cells come in two classes and five types: the granulocytes and the agranulocytes (monocytes and lymphocytes), each with its share, most to least common, its nucleus and its line in the hematopoiesis tree

stem: True or false: Neutrophils are the most common white cell in normal blood and the body's first line of defense against bacteria.
