why: Neutrophils are 50 to 70 percent of the white cells, the blood's main phagocyte and the first line of defense against bacteria.
Both halves hold: neutrophils are the most common white cell (50 to 70 percent; lymphocytes are next at 30 to 40) and the first line of defense against bacteria.

likely.t: The white cells' jobs: the neutrophil (multi-lobed, the first line of defense against bacteria), eosinophil (red granules, major basic protein against parasites, allergy), basophil (dark blue granules, heparin, asthma) and monocyte (becomes the macrophage)

stem: Which two white cells are the agranulocytes?
ex: He said what you need to remember is two classes and five types. The granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) have prominent granules; the agranulocytes (monocytes and lymphocytes) don't. He asked the class whether lymphocytes are granulocytes or agranulocytes: agranulocytes.
why: The agranulocytes lack prominent granules: the monocytes and the lymphocytes (B, T and NK cells).
Neutrophils and eosinophils both have prominent granules: they are two of the three granulocytes.
Eosinophils and basophils are granulocytes, with large red or dark blue granules.
Basophils are granulocytes, with large dark blue granules; the monocyte is an agranulocyte, but its partner is the lymphocyte.

likely.t: Recognizing the blood cells and their jobs: red cells (most of the cells) carry oxygen and carbon dioxide, platelets come from megakaryocytes ("just knowledge you should know") and start clotting, and the white cells come in two classes and five types: the granulocytes and the agranulocytes (monocytes and lymphocytes), each with its share, most to least common, its nucleus and its line in the hematopoiesis tree

stem: He said that when you hear the word "humoral," you should think of which response?
choices: The B cell response and its antibodies
The T cell response to transformed cells
The NK cell response to cells without MHC I
The neutrophil response to invading bacteria
ex: His shortcut: "When you hear the word humoral, think B-cell response. And then also, when you hear B cells, think about the production of antibodies." The cellular response is the T cells', and the two arms act together.
why: Humoral means the B cells: they make the antibodies that mark invaders for destruction by other cells.
Targeting transformed and virus-infected cells is the cellular response, which belongs to the T cells.
Killing cells that lack MHC class I is the NK cell's innate job, not the humoral response.
Neutrophils are innate phagocytes, the first line of defense against bacteria, not the humoral arm.

likely.t: Innate versus adaptive immunity: what the body just does (barriers, low pH, lysozyme, thiocyanate, interferons, phagocytes, NK cells), versus the antibodies of the humoral arm ("think B-cell response") and the T cells of the cellular arm

stem: A B cell's surface antibody binds the antigen it fits. What happens next, as he described it?
choices: It recruits helper T cells and becomes a plasma cell that releases that antibody
It travels to the thymus, where positive selection checks it against self MHC
It shows the antigen on MHC class I so an NK cell can kill it and end the reaction
It secretes perforins into the cell that carries the antigen, as a cytotoxic T cell would
ex: His drawing: a B cell whose antibody doesn't fit an antigen can't bind it, but one that fits does. The binding generates a chemical signal that recruits helper T cells, and the B cell transforms into a plasma cell, makes a great many antibodies like the one that bound, and releases them into the circulation.
why: Binding sends a chemical signal that recruits helper T cells; the B cell becomes a plasma cell that makes many antibodies like the one that bound and releases them into the circulation.
The thymus educates T cells, not B cells; self-reactive B cells are removed in the bone marrow.
NK cells kill cells missing MHC class I; a B cell that meets its antigen is activated, not killed.
Perforins are the cytotoxic T cell's weapon; a B cell's weapon is the antibody, secreted once it becomes a plasma cell.

likely.t: B and T cells: a B cell whose antibody fits an antigen recruits helper T cells and becomes a plasma cell that releases that antibody, in a secondary organ; helper T cells help the B cells, cytotoxic T cells kill what they bind, and T cells carry memory

stem: Why doesn't an NK cell kill the body's healthy cells?
choices: Their MHC class I binds its inhibitory receptor, which stops the killing
They carry no activating ligand for its activating receptor to bind
Its antigen-specific receptor recognizes them as self, as a T cell's does
Healthy cells are coated with IgG, which its CD16 receptor reads as a safe signal
ex: His NK schematic: the healthy cell shows an activating ligand and MHC class I. The NK cell's activating receptor wants to bind the ligand, but its inhibitory receptor binds the MHC class I and stops that response, so the healthy cell is spared. A cell missing its MHC class I is killed.
why: In his schematic the healthy cell shows MHC class I; the NK cell's inhibitory receptor binds it and stops the response, so there is no killing.
The healthy cell does have the activating ligand, and the activating receptor wants to bind it; the MHC class I is what holds it back.
NK cells lack specific antigen receptors; that kind of self recognition belongs to T cells.
IgG bound to CD16 marks a target for ADCC, the opposite of a safe signal.

likely.t: NK cells: no B or T markers and no specific receptors; MHC class I on a healthy cell binds the inhibitory receptor and stops the killing, a cell missing it is killed, and too many activating ligands cause induced killing; in ADCC, CD16 binds IgG's constant region

stem:
Which statements about how an NK cell decides to kill are true?
1. A tumor or virus-infected cell that has lost its MHC class I is killed.
2. NK cells recognize their targets through specific antigen receptors, like B and T cells.
3. Many more activating ligands than usual can make an NK cell kill a cell that still shows MHC class I.
4. The NK cell's activating receptor binds an activating ligand on the other cell.
ex: His three scenarios: a healthy cell shows MHC class I, which binds the NK cell's inhibitory receptor, so no killing; a target cell (tumor or virus-infected) keeps the activating ligand but is missing MHC class I, so the activating receptor wins and it is killed; and with many more activating ligands, induced killing of even a self cell, probably part of autoimmune responses. NK cells have no specific antigen receptors.
why: It leaves out 4, which is true: the activating receptor binds the activating ligand, and that is the signal to kill.
Statements 1, 3 and 4 are true. Statement 2 is false: NK cells lack specific antigen receptors, and the B and T cell markers.
It includes 2, which is false: NK cells lack specific antigen receptors. It leaves out 1, which is true: a cell missing MHC class I is killed.
It leaves out 1, which is true: a target cell missing MHC class I is killed, because nothing engages the inhibitory receptor.

likely.t: NK cells: no B or T markers and no specific receptors; MHC class I on a healthy cell binds the inhibitory receptor and stops the killing, a cell missing it is killed, and too many activating ligands cause induced killing; in ADCC, CD16 binds IgG's constant region

stem: In his schematic of a lymph node, which route does the lymph take?
choices: Afferent lymphatic, subcapsular sinus, trabecular sinuses, efferent lymphatic
Efferent lymphatic, trabecular sinuses, subcapsular sinus, then the afferent lymphatic
Afferent lymphatic, high endothelial venule, paracortex, splenic vein
Splenic artery, marginal sinus, penicillar arterioles, efferent lymphatic
ex: He followed the lymph: an afferent lymphatic vessel, with valves that direct the flow, empties into the subcapsular sinus; the lymph runs into the trabecular sinuses (with the chance to pass a germinal center), and it leaves in the efferent lymphatic vessel.
why: Lymph comes in an afferent lymphatic (its valves direct the flow), runs into the subcapsular sinus under the capsule, then the trabecular sinuses, and leaves in the efferent lymphatic.
That runs it backward: afferent vessels bring lymph in and the efferent vessel takes it out.
High endothelial venules are where lymphocytes from the blood enter a node, and the splenic vein drains the spleen.
The splenic artery, marginal sinuses and penicillar arterioles are the spleen's blood supply; the spleen has no afferent lymphatics.

likely.t: The lymph node: the lymph's route (afferent lymphatic, subcapsular sinus, trabecular sinuses, efferent lymphatic); activation in the paracortex and follicles, B cells multiplying in germinal centers and plasma cells secreting antibody in the medulla

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. In a lymph node, the initial T and B cell activation takes place in the paracortex.
2. In a lymph node's medulla, plasma cells secrete antibody.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: His walk through a node: the antigen comes in the afferent lymphatic; initial T and B cell activation in the paracortex; B cell activation in a primary follicle; B cell proliferation and differentiation in the germinal center; plasma cells secreting antibody in the medulla; and out the efferent lymphatic.
why: Statement 1 is true: he placed the initial T and B cell activation in the paracortex. Statement 2 is true: the medulla is where plasma cells secrete antibody.
Statement 1 is true, not false: the initial T and B cell activation is in the paracortex. Statement 2 is true, not false: plasma cells secrete antibody in the medulla.
Statement 2 is true, not false: plasma cells secrete their antibody in the medulla, and it leaves in the efferent lymphatic.
Statement 1 is true, not false: the first T and B cell activation happens in the paracortex, before the follicles.

likely.t: The lymph node: the lymph's route (afferent lymphatic, subcapsular sinus, trabecular sinuses, efferent lymphatic); activation in the paracortex and follicles, B cells multiplying in germinal centers and plasma cells secreting antibody in the medulla

stem: Which supporting cell of a lymph node monitors for foreign particles and presents them to T cells?
ex: A node's supporting cells, as he listed them: reticular cells secrete type III collagen and the stroma's matrix; dendritic cells are antigen-presenting cells that monitor foreign particles and present them to T cells; macrophages phagocytose; follicular dendritic cells' hair-like processes interdigitate between the B cells of germinal centers.
why: Dendritic cells, with their many tentacle-like processes, are antigen-presenting cells: they watch for foreign particles and present them to T cells.
Follicular dendritic cells reach between the B cells of germinal centers and hold antigen-antibody complexes; they lack MHC II and present nothing.
Reticular cells secrete the type III collagen and matrix of the stroma.
Plasma cells secrete antibody, in the medulla; they don't present antigen to T cells.

stem: Which tonsils lie at the torus tubarius, where the auditory tube opens into the nasopharynx?
ex: On his sagittal section of the head: the pharyngeal tonsil in the back of the nasal cavity, the tubal tonsils at the torus tubarius where the auditory tube comes in, the palatine tonsils in the back of the throat, and the lingual tonsils on the back of the tongue.
why: The tubal tonsils sit by the torus tubarius, at the opening of the auditory tube.
The palatine tonsils are the pair in the back of the throat, the ones often removed.
The lingual tonsils are on the back of the tongue, which is why it looks rough.
The pharyngeal tonsil (the adenoid) is in the back of the nasal cavity, near the tubal tonsils but not at the tube's opening.

stem: Which statement about the tonsils is true?
choices: Tonsillar crypts trap material so the tissue has longer to respond
The lingual tonsils sit in the back of the nasal cavity, above the soft palate
The tonsils are primary lymphoid organs, where T cells are first educated
The tonsils have both afferent and efferent lymphatic vessels
ex: The tonsils are aggregates of lymphoid tissue, part of MALT and so secondary lymphoid organs. They sit where you breathe and eat, so they start the response early, and the palatine tonsils' crypts trap material so there is more time to respond. His slide adds that they have no afferent lymphatics.
why: He said substances get wedged into the palatine tonsils' crypts, which gives the tissue a longer time to respond.
The lingual tonsils are on the back of the tongue; the pharyngeal tonsil is the one in the back of the nasal cavity.
Tonsils are MALT, a secondary lymphoid organ; the primary organs are just the bone marrow and the thymus, and the thymus educates T cells.
The tonsils have efferent lymphatics only, no afferent ones; the lymph node is the one with both.

stem: How do blood-borne antigens and lymphocytes get into the spleen?
choices: In the splenic artery, a branch of the celiac trunk, at the hilum
In afferent lymphatic vessels that pierce the capsule all around the organ
In the splenic vein, which enters at the hilum
Through the thoracic duct, which drains into it
ex: The spleen, a secondary lymphoid organ, filters blood. He said the large splenic artery comes off the celiac trunk and goes into the hilum, carrying the blood-borne antigens and lymphocytes in. The splenic vein leaves at the hilum, and there are no afferent lymphatics.
why: He said the splenic artery comes off the celiac trunk into the hilum and carries the blood-borne antigens and lymphocytes in.
The spleen has no afferent lymphatics: it filters blood, not lymph.
The splenic vein drains the spleen; it leaves at the hilum.
The thoracic duct collects lymph and drains into the subclavian veins, not the spleen.

stem: A periarteriolar lymphatic sheath (PALS) around a central artery tells you that you are looking at which organ?
ex: "The main thing is just to really associate this PALS with the spleen," he said, and: "If you see a central artery, that's where you have that area of PALS." The PALS is the T cell area of the spleen's white pulp.
why: He said to associate the PALS with the spleen: the T cell sheath around the central artery of the white pulp.
A lymph node's T cells are in the paracortex, with high endothelial venules; it has no PALS.
The thymus has a cortex and medulla, with Hassall's corpuscles in the medulla; it has no PALS.
A Peyer's patch is lymphoid nodules in the wall of the ileum, under M cells; its T cells sit between the nodules.

likely.t: The spleen: the PALS, the T cell sheath around the central artery ("associate this PALS with the spleen"); white pulp and red pulp; and what the spleen does

stem: True or false: GALT counts as a primary lymphoid organ, along with the bone marrow and the thymus.
ex: His overview figure lists GALT with the primary organs, and he said: "We're not going to consider GALT as a primary lymphatic organ, but we will consider the thymus and the bone marrow as our primary lymphoid organs." Every other lymphoid organ, GALT included, is secondary.
why: He crossed GALT off the primary list on his figure: for this class the primary organs are just the bone marrow and the thymus.
The statement is false: GALT is secondary; the only primary lymphoid organs are the bone marrow and the thymus.

likely.t: Primary versus secondary lymphoid organs: the primary ones are just the bone marrow and the thymus (not GALT), where B and T cells become immunocompetent without antigen ("bone marrow, B cells, thymus, T cells"); every other one, lymph nodes, MALT and GALT, and the spleen, is secondary

stem: True or false: NK cells are the small lymphocytes, and B and T cells are the large ones.
ex: Lymphocytes come in two sizes: the NK cells are "pretty large," and the B and T cells "a little bit smaller." Either way the nucleus takes up most of the cell, with a thin rim of cytoplasm.
why: That's swapped: he said the NK cells are pretty large and the B and T cells a little smaller.
The statement is false: the NK cells are the large lymphocytes, and the B and T cells are the small ones.

stem: True or false: The walls of the splenic sinuses have no smooth muscle and no pericytes.
ex: The splenic sinuses are sinusoidal vessels lined by rod-shaped, loosely packed endothelial cells, with macrophage processes reaching between them and strands of basal lamina looping around them at right angles. There's no smooth muscle and no pericytes.
why: He said there's no smooth muscle and no pericytes in the splenic sinuses: rod-shaped endothelial cells, macrophage processes and strands of basal lamina at right angles.
The statement is true: the splenic sinuses have no smooth muscle and no pericytes.

stem: A patient has a firm, enlarged lymph node in the neck, and lymphoma is suspected. What makes the diagnosis?
choices: Sampling of tissue, such as the lymph node or the bone marrow
A CT scan showing enlarged nodes in more than one region
A routine blood count showing a raised lymphocyte count
The B symptoms: fever, drenching night sweats and weight loss
ex: He said that when lymphoma is suspected, the tissue has to be sampled: a biopsy, or better the whole node excised. Enlarged nodes and even B symptoms have other causes (reactive and infectious nodes, lupus, tuberculosis), so only the tissue, read with immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry, makes the diagnosis.
why: A tissue sample gives the morphology, immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry that diagnose and classify a lymphoma.
Imaging shows where the disease is, which matters for staging, but it can't say what the cells are.
A blood count can raise the suspicion (CLL is the one diagnosed from the blood), but a lymphoma in a node is diagnosed from tissue.
B symptoms are high-yield clues, but infections such as tuberculosis cause them too, so he said you still sample the tissue.

likely.t: The B symptoms, his "high-yield clues" (a fever of 38 °C or more, drenching night sweats, losing 10 percent of body weight in 6 months): they raise the suspicion, and the tissue makes the diagnosis

stem:
Which of these are B symptoms of lymphoma, as he defined them?
1. A fever of 38 °C or higher with no obvious cause
2. Unexplained weight loss of at least 5 percent of body weight over the past year
3. Night sweats that soak the bedding and clothes
4. Bone pain from the marrow expanding
ex: He called the B symptoms "really high-yield clues" of lymphoma: a fever of 38 °C or higher, drenching night sweats that soak the sheets (not light ones), and unexplained weight loss of at least 10 percent of body weight over the past 6 months.
why: It includes 2, which is false: the B-symptom weight loss is at least 10 percent of body weight over the past 6 months.

Statements 1 and 3 are true. Statement 2 is false: the weight loss is at least 10 percent over the past 6 months. Statement 4 is false: bone pain from marrow expansion is a sign of leukemia, not a B symptom.
It includes 4, which is false: bone pain from marrow expansion is a feature of leukemia's organ infiltration, not a B symptom.
It includes 4, which is false: bone pain from marrow expansion belongs to leukemia. It leaves out 1, which is true: a fever of 38 °C or higher without an obvious cause.

likely.t: The B symptoms, his "high-yield clues" (a fever of 38 °C or more, drenching night sweats, losing 10 percent of body weight in 6 months): they raise the suspicion, and the tissue makes the diagnosis

stem: Which finding in an excised lymph node points to lymphoma rather than a benign node?
choices: Architecture effaced by one monotonous population of cells
Open (patent) sinuses with macrophages in them
Separate follicles with germinal centers, confined to the outer cortex
ex: He said a benign node is well circumscribed and rubbery, with B-cell follicles and germinal centers in the cortex, T-cell areas deeper in, and open (patent) sinuses holding macrophages. A lymphoma node is fleshy and plump, and its architecture is effaced: replaced by a monotonous population of similar cells.
why: Effaced architecture, wiped out by a monotonous population of similar cells, is the general sign of lymphoma he gave.
Patent sinuses, where the macrophages live and the lymphocytes pass through, are a clue that the node is benign.
Follicles with germinal centers in the cortex are where normal B cells belong; crowded back-to-back follicles would be follicular lymphoma.
A well-circumscribed, rubbery node is how he described a normal one; a lymphoma node looks fleshy and plump.

stem: Flow cytometry of an enlarged node finds that nearly all its B cells carry kappa light chains and almost none carry lambda. What does that point to?
choices: A clonal B-cell population: a lymphoma
A reactive node responding to an infection
A T-cell lymphoma growing in the node
Acute myeloid leukemia spreading to the node
ex: He said each B cell carries either kappa or lambda, and a normal node has both, about 3 kappa to 1 lambda. A lymphoma's cells all share one abnormality, so they show only kappa or only lambda: "that's a clue that I'm looking at something that's what we call clonal."
why: Only one light chain means the B cells are clonal, the offspring of one abnormal cell: a B-cell lymphoma.
A reactive node keeps the normal mix of kappa and lambda B cells, about 3 to 1.
Kappa and lambda are on B cells; a clonal kappa-only population is a B-cell tumor, not a T-cell one.
AML is myeloid blasts; kappa and lambda are B-cell light chains.

stem: Which cell gives rise to most lymphoid neoplasms?
choices: B and T cells equally (about half each)
ex: The vast majority of lymphoid neoplasms, 85 to 90 percent, are of B-cell origin. The rest are T-cell neoplasms, and tumors of NK-cell origin are only rarely encountered.
why: B cells give rise to 85 to 90 percent of lymphoid neoplasms.
T-cell neoplasms are the remainder, about 10 to 15 percent.
Tumors of NK-cell origin are rare.
The split is lopsided: 85 to 90 percent B-cell, the rest nearly all T-cell.

stem: He said each lymphoma arises from a normal counterpart in the node. Which lymphoma arises from the B cells of the germinal centers?
ex: He said the germinal centers give follicular lymphoma; just around them, the mantle zone gives mantle cell lymphoma; and around the mantle, the marginal zone gives marginal zone lymphoma. The thymus does the same for the T-cell lymphomas.
why: Follicular lymphoma arises from germinal center B cells.
Mantle cell lymphoma arises from the mantle zone, just around the germinal center.
Marginal zone lymphoma arises from the marginal zone, outside the mantle.
Mycosis fungoides is a T-cell lymphoma of the skin, not a follicle B-cell tumor.

likely.t: Lymphoma categories, his closing point: which lymphomas are B-cell and which T-cell, which are indolent and which aggressive, and the part of the follicle each B-cell lymphoma comes from

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Classic Hodgkin lymphoma often involves the peripheral blood.
2. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma can skip node groups, with enlarged nodes above and below the diaphragm and a normal-sized node between them.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: He contrasted the two: Hodgkin lymphoma is usually localized, spreads contiguously from one node to the next, rarely goes outside the nodes and never involves the peripheral blood; non-Hodgkin lymphoma is usually widespread, may spread non-contiguously, goes outside the nodes much more often and can involve the blood.
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: he said the peripheral blood is never involved by Hodgkin lymphoma.
Statement 2 is true, not false: non-Hodgkin lymphoma can spread non-contiguously, skipping a node group.
Statement 1 is false, not true: the blood is not involved in Hodgkin lymphoma. Statement 2 is true, not false: non-Hodgkin lymphoma can skip node groups.

Statement 1 is false: he said the peripheral blood is never involved by Hodgkin lymphoma. Statement 2 is true: non-Hodgkin lymphoma may spread non-contiguously, above and below the diaphragm with the node between them not enlarged.

likely.t: Hodgkin versus non-Hodgkin: Hodgkin is usually localized, spreads contiguously, rarely leaves the nodes and never involves the blood, with a few large Reed-Sternberg cells; non-Hodgkin lymphoma is usually widespread, can skip node groups, often starts outside the nodes, can reach the blood, and is mostly B-cell

stem: In lymphoma staging, which finding makes the disease stage 4, the most advanced?
choices: Disseminated disease, such as in the marrow or liver
Nodes involved on both sides of the diaphragm
Two or more node regions on the same side of the diaphragm
B symptoms such as fever and drenching night sweats
ex: He said staging asks whether one site or several are involved, above or below the diaphragm or on both sides, whether there are sites outside the nodes or lymphatic system, or whether it is disseminated: "that's the stage 4 disease, and that's the most aggressive." The letter B after a stage marks B symptoms.
why: Disseminated disease through organs outside the lymphatic system, such as the marrow or liver, is stage 4.
Nodes on both sides of the diaphragm is stage 3 on the standard chart.
Several node regions on one side of the diaphragm is stage 2 on the standard chart.
B symptoms add the letter B to the stage; they don't set the stage's number.

stem: True or false: Leukemia frequently starts in the bone marrow and can extend to the spleen, liver and lymph nodes.
ex: He said leukemia generally involves the bone marrow and the blood, as lymphoma generally involves the nodes. It frequently starts in the marrow and can extend to the reticuloendothelial system (spleen, liver, lymph nodes); untreated, it is fatal.
why: It frequently starts in the bone marrow and can extend to the reticuloendothelial system: the spleen, liver and lymph nodes.
The statement is right: marrow first, then the spleen, liver, lymph nodes and other tissues.

stem: In the neutrophil line, which cell comes right after the promyelocyte?
ex: He walked the ladder aloud: myeloblast, promyelocyte (granules appear), myelocyte (the chromatin turns clumped and coarse), band, then the segmented neutrophil (PMN), the cell released into the blood. His slide puts the metamyelocyte between the myelocyte and the band. In APL, maturation stops at the promyelocyte.
why: The myelocyte follows the promyelocyte.
The metamyelocyte comes after the myelocyte.
The myeloblast is the earliest cell, before the promyelocyte.
The band is the last stage before the segmented neutrophil.

stem: Acute leukemia causes symptoms two ways: marrow failure and organ infiltration. Each of the following comes from marrow failure EXCEPT:
ex: He split leukemia's symptoms into marrow failure (fatigue, malaise and pallor from anemia; bruising and bleeding from too few platelets; fever and infection from too few working white cells) and cells growing in tissues (bone pain, an enlarged spleen, liver or nodes, and gingival hypertrophy, where he said a dentist may be the first clue).
why: Gingival hypertrophy comes from organ infiltration: leukemic cells growing in the gums, like the bone pain and the enlarged spleen, liver and nodes.
Pallor and fatigue come from the anemia of a failing marrow.
Bruising and bleeding come from too few platelets as the marrow fails.
Fever and infections come from too few working white cells as the marrow fails.

likely.t: Acute versus chronic leukemia (onset, course, blasts, platelets, organomegaly) and leukemia's clinical consequences: marrow failure (anemia, bleeding, infection) and cells growing in tissues (bone pain, spleen, liver, nodes, and the gums, where a dentist may be the first clue)

stem: Which site is used for both the core biopsy and the aspirate of bone marrow in an adult?
ex: He said: in adults, the posterior iliac crest, for the core biopsy and the aspirate; in small children, the tibia, aspirate only; and if neither can be used, a sternal aspirate, never a core, because the heart lies right below.
why: The posterior iliac crest gives both the biopsy and the aspirate.
The sternum gives an aspirate only: no core biopsy there, because the heart lies right below.
The tibia is used for an aspirate only, and only in small children.
The mandible is not one of his marrow sampling sites.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Acute leukemia has a rapid onset and, untreated, runs a course of less than 6 months.
2. Chronic myeloid leukemia has a rapid onset and, untreated, runs a course of 2 to 6 years.
choices: Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Acute leukemia: rapid onset, under 6 months untreated. Chronic myeloid leukemia: insidious onset, 2 to 6 years untreated. Untreated, both end in death by infection or bleeding.
why: Statement 2 is false, not true: chronic myeloid leukemia has an insidious onset; the rapid onset belongs to acute leukemia.
Statement 1 is true, not false: acute leukemia comes on rapidly and, untreated, runs less than 6 months.
Statement 1 is true: acute leukemia comes on rapidly and, untreated, runs less than 6 months. Statement 2 is false: chronic myeloid leukemia comes on insidiously (its 2 to 6 years is right).
Statement 1 is true, not false: acute leukemia comes on rapidly and runs less than 6 months untreated. Statement 2 is false, not true: chronic myeloid leukemia comes on insidiously.

likely.t: Acute versus chronic leukemia (onset, course, blasts, platelets, organomegaly) and leukemia's clinical consequences: marrow failure (anemia, bleeding, infection) and cells growing in tissues (bone pain, spleen, liver, nodes, and the gums, where a dentist may be the first clue)

stem: Which statement comparing acute leukemia with chronic myeloid leukemia is false?
choices: Acute leukemia shows mostly mature cells, with fewer than 20 percent blasts
Chronic myeloid leukemia shows prominent organomegaly
Platelets are low to very low in acute leukemia
In chronic myeloid leukemia, platelets are normal or raised early, then fall
ex: He said the key finding in acute leukemia is blasts, greater than 20 percent, with platelets that are usually severely low; in chronic myeloid leukemia the blasts are under 20 percent, usually much less, the white count is high, the anemia and low platelets are milder, and the organs can be enlarged. His slide adds that CML's platelets start normal or high.
why: This is the false one: acute leukemia is immature cells, blasts, over 20 percent of the marrow; mature cells with fewer than 20 percent blasts is chronic leukemia.
This is true: chronic leukemia brings prominent organomegaly; acute leukemia only mild.
This is true: acute leukemia leaves the platelets low to very low.
This is true: in chronic leukemia the platelets start normal or high, then fall.

likely.t: Acute versus chronic leukemia (onset, course, blasts, platelets, organomegaly) and leukemia's clinical consequences: marrow failure (anemia, bleeding, infection) and cells growing in tissues (bone pain, spleen, liver, nodes, and the gums, where a dentist may be the first clue)

stem: For most types of AML, what blast percentage in the marrow or blood is the diagnostic threshold?
ex: He said greater than 20 percent blasts, in the blood or the marrow, is "our threshold for making the diagnosis" (the WHO writes 20 percent or more). An AML with one of its defining genetic abnormalities is diagnosed whatever the blast count.
why: Most AML needs 20 percent blasts; fewer, with abnormal counts, points to a disorder such as MDS.
5 percent is the low end of his acute leukemia range for blasts in the blood, but the AML threshold is 20 percent.
He gave 20 percent as the threshold; 10 percent isn't one.
Blasts can reach 95 percent, but 20 percent is enough for the diagnosis.

likely.t: AML's diagnostic threshold (more than 20 percent blasts), Auer rods (a myeloid blast, never ALL), and AML in adults versus ALL in children

stem: True or false: When AML carries one of its defining genetic abnormalities, it can be diagnosed whatever the blast count.
ex: He said there are two ways to diagnose AML: with a specific cytogenetic abnormality, "you don't even have to have 20% blasts"; without one, you need the 20 percent.
why: With one of the defining genetic abnormalities, AML can be diagnosed no matter the blast count.
The statement is right: the 20 percent rule is for the AML types without a defining genetic abnormality.

stem: Which statement about AML and ALL is true?
choices: AML is mainly a disease of adults, with a median age of about 65
ALL is mainly a disease of adults, with a peak at 60 to 65
Lymphoblasts carry granules and Auer rods
Myeloblasts are small cells with scant cytoplasm and indistinct nucleoli
ex: He said AML is more common in adults (median age 65) and rare in children, with medium to large blasts that may hold Auer rods; ALL is mostly children, usually 1 to 5 years old, with small to medium blasts, very little cytoplasm, no granules and no Auer rods.
why: AML is common in adults, with a median age of 65, and relatively rare in children.
ALL is common in children, highest at 1 to 5 years with a peak at 2 to 3, and less common in adults.
Lymphoblasts have no granules, and Auer rods exclude ALL; granules and Auer rods belong to myeloblasts.
That describes lymphoblasts; myeloblasts are medium to large, with moderate cytoplasm and distinct nucleoli.

likely.t: AML's diagnostic threshold (more than 20 percent blasts), Auer rods (a myeloid blast, never ALL), and AML in adults versus ALL in children

stem: What is an Auer rod?

stem: In follicular lymphoma, what does the t(14;18) translocation do?

stem: A 68-year-old man's enlarged lymph nodes show a lymphoma that carries t(11;14). Which lymphoma is it?

stem: Which lymphoma is most likely?

stem: True or false: Stage for stage, breast cancer in men has a much worse prognosis than in women.
ex: The slide: breast carcinoma in men is extremely rare and usually advanced at presentation, but stage for stage it has the same prognosis as in women, and the patient may have a family history (BRCA2).
why: The statement is wrong: stage for stage the prognosis is the same; men do worse only because their cancer is found later.
The slide: stage for stage, the same prognosis as female breast cancer; it is usually advanced at presentation because men aren't screened.
